explanations.explanation: Eight hundred, friend. Josheb-basshebeth, chief of the Three, wields his spear against eight hundred men and kills them at one time (2 Samuel 23:8). That's the number the writer gives. I've stamped some big batches in my day, but I've never had to count to eight hundred and keep a straight face.

Two hundred is a big number, but the verse goes higher. It says Josheb-basshebeth, the chief of the Three, wields his spear against eight hundred men and kills them at one time. Don't feel bad. Even I had to read that one twice and ask if the number got stuck.

One thousand sounds like a nice round number, and the verse stops short of it. The text says Josheb-basshebeth wields his spear against eight hundred men, whom he kills at one time. He's chief of the Three, so eight hundred is plenty to earn the title.

That's it! Eleazar son of Dodo stands his ground and strikes the Philistines until his hand grows weary and sticks to his sword (2 Samuel 23:10). The men of Israel are retreating, and he plants his feet anyway. I can barely hold a stamp for a whole batch, and this man's hand wouldn't let go of a sword.

Falling back is what the men of Israel do. The verse before says they retreated (2 Samuel 23:9). Eleazar does the opposite: he stands his ground and strikes the Philistines until his hand grows weary and sticks to his sword.

The text never has Eleazar running anywhere for orders. It says he went with David to taunt the Philistines (2 Samuel 23:9). Then, while the men of Israel retreat, Eleazar stands his ground and strikes the Philistines until his hand grows weary and sticks to his sword.

Yes, the LORD. The verse says, "The LORD brought about a great victory that day." Eleazar's hand was stuck to his sword, but the credit goes to the LORD. A good baker learns that quick: the oven does the baking, and I just hold the stamp.

Eleazar sure did his part. He stood his ground and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary. But the verse names who brought about the victory: "The LORD brought about a great victory that day."
David is there that day, since Eleazar went with him to taunt the Philistines. But the verse doesn't give David the credit for the victory. It says, "The LORD brought about a great victory that day."

Plunder, that's the word. The verse says the troops returned to Eleazar, "but only to plunder the dead." Nobody there is bringing a casserole. They arrive after the work is done, and I have a feeling Eleazar's sticky hand noticed.
Burying would be a different return, and the text doesn't say that. It says the troops returned to him "but only to plunder the dead." The word "only" tells you what they came back for.
Mourning isn't what brings them back. The verse says the troops returned to Eleazar "but only to plunder the dead." They had retreated earlier, then showed up for the spoils.

True. When the Philistines banded together near a field full of lentils, Israel's troops fled from them (2 Samuel 23:11). That's the third mighty man in a row facing a scary crowd. Shammah son of Agee the Hararite is about to show what he does when others run.

Close, but the verse says it plainly: when the Philistines had banded together near a field full of lentils, Israel's troops fled from them (2 Samuel 23:11). So the answer is True. And the story gets better from there, because Shammah doesn't follow the crowd.

explanations.answer: In the middle of the field
explanations.explanation: Right in the middle, baker. Shammah "took his stand in the middle of the field" (2 Samuel 23:12). The troops have fled, and he picks the spot where everybody can see him. Lentils all around his ankles, and he's not budging.

explanations.answer: At the edge of the field
explanations.explanation: The edge would be a safer spot, but that's not what the verse says. Shammah "took his stand in the middle of the field." Everyone else is running, and he plants himself right in the center.

explanations.answer: On the road past the field
explanations.explanation: The road would've been a handy exit, and Shammah doesn't take it. The verse says he "took his stand in the middle of the field." He's in the lentils, not past them.

The text says the opposite. Shammah took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines (2 Samuel 23:12). So the answer is False. The Philistines don't get the field.

False is right. Shammah took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines, so the Philistines don't take it. The verse ends, "So the LORD brought about a great victory" (2 Samuel 23:12). One man, one field, and the LORD brought the win.

Bethlehem it is. David is in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines is at Bethlehem (2 Samuel 23:14). Keep that town in mind, because the next verse is about a well by its gate. It's a long way from the kitchen, but it's the center of this whole story.
Jerusalem isn't the town in this verse. It says David was in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem. That detail matters for what David says next.
Hebron isn't named here. The verse says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem (2 Samuel 23:14). Bethlehem is the town with the well David is about to wish for.

Break through. The three mighty men "broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David" (2 Samuel 23:16). David only sighed, and they went straight through the middle. I've seen people bring me a drink of water, but never through a camp.
Sneaking around would be quieter, but that's not what the text says. The three mighty men "broke through the Philistine camp." They went right through it to reach the well.

Spying isn't in the verse. It says the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David (2 Samuel 23:16). They went in and came out with the water.
I get why you'd think so. Three men broke through a camp for that water! But the verse says David "refused to drink it" (2 Samuel 23:16). So the answer is False. What he does instead is the surprise.
False is right. The three men bring the water back, and David "refused to drink it" (2 Samuel 23:16). He pours it out to the LORD instead. After all that effort, that's a lot of water to turn down.

explanations.answer: Pours it out to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. David refused to drink it and "poured it out to the LORD" (2 Samuel 23:16). He doesn't give it back or keep it. I think he's treating that water as something special.

explanations.answer: Gives it back to the three
explanations.explanation: David doesn't hand it back to the three. The verse says he refused to drink it and poured it out to the LORD (2 Samuel 23:16). It's a quiet moment after a loud trip.

explanations.answer: Saves it for the next battle
explanations.explanation: Saving it isn't in the story. The verse says David refused to drink it and "poured it out to the LORD." The water goes out right there.

explanations.answer: His men risked their lives for it
explanations.explanation: Right, and David says so himself: "Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?" (2 Samuel 23:17). He wished for the water, but he won't drink what cost his men that much. I think that tells you how David sees the three who went.

explanations.answer: He fears the well is poisoned
explanations.explanation: Poison is never mentioned. David gives his reason in his own words: "Far be it from me, O LORD, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?" (2 Samuel 23:17). His men risked their lives, and that's why he won't drink it.

explanations.answer: He vowed to fast until evening
explanations.explanation: A fast isn't mentioned here. David says, "Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?" (2 Samuel 23:17). That's his reason, and it comes straight from his mouth.

Joab it is. Abishai son of Zeruiah is the brother of Joab (2 Samuel 23:18), and Joab son of Zeruiah was over David's army (2 Samuel 8:16). Two brothers, both in David's story. I've only ever had a drawer full of strangers, so that's a lot of family for one honor roll.
Abner is a different man. He was Saul's army commander, Saul's uncle (1 Samuel 14:50). The verse says Abishai is the brother of Joab, who was over David's army (2 Samuel 8:16).
Amasa is someone else. He's the man Absalom put over the army in place of Joab (2 Samuel 17:25). Abishai's brother is Joab, who was over David's army (2 Samuel 8:16).

Three hundred, baker. Abishai wields his spear against three hundred men, kills them, and wins a name along with the Three (2 Samuel 23:18). That's fewer than Josheb-basshebeth's eight hundred, and still plenty to get a name on the list. You were paying attention.

Six hundred is more than the verse says. Abishai wields his spear against three hundred men, kills them, and wins a name along with the Three. Easy to mix up with the eight hundred earlier, since these numbers all sound alike.

Five hundred is a good guess, but the verse says three hundred. Abishai wields his spear against three hundred men and wins a name along with the Three (2 Samuel 23:18). It's a number that sticks once you hear it a second time.

A lion! Benaiah, a man of valor from Kabzeel, goes down into a pit on a snowy day and kills a lion (2 Samuel 23:20). A pit, a lion and snow all in one verse. That's three things I'd avoid in a single day.
A bear would be scary, but it's not the animal here. Benaiah goes down into a pit on a snowy day and kills a lion (2 Samuel 23:20). The pit and the snow are the details that stand out.
The verse doesn't say wolf. Benaiah goes down into a pit on a snowy day and kills a lion (2 Samuel 23:20). It's a story you'd remember because of how many odd details are packed in.

True. Even though the Egyptian is a huge man with a spear in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club (2 Samuel 23:21). A club against a spear sounds like a bad deal on paper. Benaiah goes anyway.

Benaiah doesn't back away. The verse says that although the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club (2 Samuel 23:21). So the answer is True. He steps up to a huge man with only a club.

explanations.answer: Snatches the spear and uses it
explanations.explanation: That's it! Benaiah "snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear" (2 Samuel 23:21). He goes in with a club and comes out with the other man's spear. That's the kind of trade I wish I could make at a yard sale.

explanations.answer: Knocks him down with the club
explanations.explanation: The club is what Benaiah brings, but it's not how the verse ends. He snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear (2 Samuel 23:21). That's the twist in the story.

explanations.answer: Calls in the guard to help
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any help. It says Benaiah went against the Egyptian with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed him with his own spear (2 Samuel 23:21). The guard shows up later, when David puts Benaiah over it.

It sounds like he should be, but the text says otherwise. Benaiah "was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three" (2 Samuel 23:23). So the answer is False. He still wins a name along with the three mighty men (2 Samuel 23:22).

False is right. Benaiah "was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three" (2 Samuel 23:23). He still wins a name along with the three mighty men (2 Samuel 23:22). Honored, just not one of the Three.
His guard, baker. The verse says, "And David appointed him over his guard" (2 Samuel 23:23). Benaiah isn't one of the Three, but David still puts him in charge of something important. Nice work.
That's too big a job for this verse. It says David appointed Benaiah over his guard (2 Samuel 23:23). The army isn't mentioned here, only the guard.
Storehouses aren't in the text. The verse says David appointed Benaiah over his guard (2 Samuel 23:23). It's a job that fits a man who handled a lion and a spear.
